title: The context window is your whole memory
question: Where does the model keep what you told it two messages ago?
can: Budget a prompt and explain why a long document gets ignored in the middle.
one_line: An AI has zero memory of your previous message; your chat app secretly pastes your entire conversation history onto a fixed-size lunch tray on every single turn — and anything that falls off the tray or sits in the dead middle gets forgotten.

story_spine.surprise: The model on the server never remembers what you told it 10 seconds ago. Every time you press Send in a chat app, the app invisibly bundles Message 1, Reply 1, Message 2, Reply 2, and Message 3 into one giant prompt and sends the whole thing from scratch.
story_spine.broken: Believing that a '128k or 1M context window' means you can dump 500 messy pages into a prompt and the model will read every line with equal care. In reality, recall accuracy drops in a steep U-curve for facts buried in the middle of a long prompt ('Lost in the Middle').
story_spine.question: What happens when a conversation grows longer than the context window tray, and why does an LLM pay sharp attention to the very beginning and very end of a document while skimming the middle?
story_spine.turn: Simulating a 24-word sliding context tray and the U-shaped recall curve in Python made me change how I structure every prompt: put critical rules and key facts at the very top and the very bottom — never buried in paragraph 14.
story_spine.payoff: You can budget prompt tokens across system instructions, RAG documents,chat history, and completion output, and place your most important facts where recall is 93% instead of 38.7%.
story_spine.honest_limit: Now we know *where* tokens sit on the tray, and earlier we saw how the model rolls a die for the next token. Next inside Academic Hall 0 (Room 105 · Sampling & Top-P), we open the full decoding toolkit.

sections.heading: Explain it like I'm 12: The Amnesia Chef and the Fixed-Size Lunch Tray
sections.body_md:
Remember from Lesson 1 that the AI's neural weights are frozen on disk? The moment an LLM finishes replying to you, it has **100% amnesia**. The model itself is completely **stateless** — it stores zero memory of your chat inside its weights.

Then how does a chat app remember what you said three turns ago? Because the app pulls off a sleight-of-hand trick: every time you hit **Send**, your client silently packs `System Rules + Turn 1 + Reply 1 + Turn 2 + Reply 2 + Your New Message` into one giant array and sends the entire script from scratch on a fixed-size tray called the **context window**.

**What shares the tray?** Everything! Your system prompt, tool/JSON schemas, retrieved RAG documents, chat history, **the model's visible reply**, *and* any **hidden reasoning/thinking tokens** (used by reasoning models like o3, Claude extended thinking, or DeepSeek-R1) all count against the exact same ceiling.

Look at Step 1 of our lab (`Figure 1`): our toy tray holds at most **24 words**. In Turn 1 you share `'My secret locker code is 7492.'` By Turn 5, the conversation overflows 24 words, so FIFO **truncation** silently shoves Turns 1–3 off the left edge. When Turn 5 asks for the locker code, the model isn't 'being dumb' — Turn 1 literally isn't in the HTTP payload!
sections.expert_note: Production memory strategies when chats exceed the tray: (1) **Sliding Window (FIFO)** drops oldest turns — simple, loses early facts; (2) **Rolling Summary** periodically compresses old turns into a concise memory block; (3) **External Vector/Graph Memory (RAG)** stores key user facts in a database and retrieves only relevant ones back onto the tray.

sections.heading: The Billing Shock — and the KV Prefix Caching Superpower
sections.body_md:
Re-sending the whole script every turn creates two huge engineering consequences:

1. **You pay for Turn 1 ten times (unless you cache the prefix!):** In Step 2 of our lab, a 10-turn chat with a 400-token system prompt and 150-token messages bills **`19,000` uncached input tokens** — paying for your system prompt and Turn 1 over and over! Modern APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, vLLM) solve this with **Prompt Caching (KV Prefix Caching)**: if the *beginning* of your prompt stays **byte-for-byte identical** across turns, the server reuses its saved Key-Value attention state and discounts those cached prefix tokens by up to **90%**, slashing our 10-turn lab bill from `19,000` down to **`3,610` effective tokens (81.0% cheaper)** — plus cutting Time-to-First-Token latency dramatically!
2. **Why giant contexts slow down (`O(N²)` self-attention):** Inside a standard Transformer, every new token attends to every earlier token. Look at Step 3 of our lab:
- `1,000` tokens → **`500,500`** attention pairs
- `10,000` tokens → **`50,005,000`** pairs (`100×` more!)
- `100,000` tokens → **`5,000,050,000`** pairs (**5 BILLION pairs!**)

Even with FlashAttention and KV caching, stuffing 100k noisy tokens onto the tray slows every call and increases memory bandwidth cost.
sections.trap_note: Common Trap — Breaking Your Own Prompt Cache! Never put a live timestamp (`Current time: 17:05:23`), random request ID, or dynamic user query at the VERY TOP of your system prompt! Changing even 1 token at byte #1 invalidates the entire downstream KV prefix cache on every single turn. Put static rules & tool schemas FIRST, dynamic info LAST.

sections.heading: Lost in the Middle & Context Rot: Why 1M Advertised ≠ 1M Effective
sections.body_md:
When models began advertising 128k–1M token windows, teams tried dumping 300 pages of messy logs into one prompt. Quality collapsed — even when everything fit comfortably on the tray.

Two landmark findings explain why:
1. **Lost in the Middle (Liu et al., Stanford 2023):** Across multi-document QA benchmarks, models recall key facts sharply when placed at the **very beginning (primacy)** or **very end (recency)** of a long context, but accuracy drops into a deep U-shaped trough in the middle. Step 4 of our lab illustrates this U-curve shape analytically (`93.0%` at Chunk 1 & 10 vs `38.7%` in Chunk 6 — explicitly modeled to visualize Liu et al.'s empirical pattern).
2. **Context Rot (Distractor Interference):** Newer frontier models score ~99% on simple 'find one exact passphrase' Needle-in-a-Haystack tests, *yet* still suffer **Context Rot** on multi-hop reasoning as you pile on loosely related distractor chunks. Every irrelevant paragraph dilutes attention weights and raises hallucination risk.
sections.expert_note: Always distinguish **advertised context limit** (the maximum sequence length the positional embeddings/RoPE accept without crashing) from **effective context length** (the length where multi-hop reasoning and instruction-following remain accurate — often a fraction of the advertised ceiling).

sections.heading: The Production Prompt Budget Formula (How to pack the tray like a pro)
sections.body_md:
Before shipping any LLM app, budget your tray explicitly:
`System + Tool Schemas + Few-Shot Examples + Retrieved Context + Chat History + Reserved Output + Reasoning Budget ≤ Context Limit`

And order your blocks from top to bottom (`Figure 3`) to win BOTH **KV Prefix Caching** AND **Primacy/Recency Attention**:
1. **Top (Static + High Primacy):** Immutable system role, formatting rules, and tool schemas. Because this block never changes between turns, it hits the **90% KV cache discount** every time.
2. **Middle (Lower Attention):** Older conversation history or secondary background documents.
3. **Bottom (Highest Recency):** Your `#1` highest-ranked retrieved document, the live timestamp/dynamic variables, and the exact user question right before generation begins.

lab.walkthrough_md:
### `build_chat_payload(history, max_tokens)`
- **What it does:** Iterates backward from the newest message (`reversed(history)`), packing turns onto the tray until `used + cost > max_tokens`, and drops everything older.
- **Why it exists:** Makes the stateless nature of LLM APIs concrete: the server never remembers Turn 1 unless your client code explicitly includes Turn 1 in the array.

### `attention_recall_probability(position_index, total_chunks)`
- **What it does:** Models the U-shaped primacy/recency curve across a 10-chunk document.
- **Why it exists:** Shows why ordering your RAG chunks matters: putting the best match at Chunk 1 or Chunk 10 yields `93.0%` recall vs `38.7%` in Chunk 6.

shareable.the_turn: Once I coded the sliding lunch tray in Python, I stopped saying 'the AI forgot what I told it' — an AI cannot forget what it never stored; either my code pushed that message off the tray, or I buried it in the middle where attention goes to sleep.
x_thread: 1/ Your AI chatbot does not remember what you said 10 seconds ago. Every time you press Send, your app secretly copies your entire conversation from Message 1 and pastes the whole script onto a fixed-size lunch tray (the context window).
2/ For Checkpoint 04 on the Campus Quad of my AI University, I simulated sliding-window truncation and the Stanford 'Lost in the Middle' U-curve in 35 lines of Python.
3/ In Turn 1 of our test chat, the user says: 'My secret locker code is 7492.' By Turn 5, the chat is 43 words long, but our toy tray only holds 24 words.

4/ To make room for Turn 5, the app silently shoves Turns 1, 2, and 3 off the back edge of the tray. When Turn 5 asks 'What was my locker code?', the model fails — because Turn 1 literally isn't in the HTTP request anymore.
5/ 'Fine,' developers say, 'I'll use a 128k or 1M context window so nothing ever falls off!' That's where the second trap hits: Lost in the Middle.

6/ When you stuff 10 chunks of text into a long prompt, the model does NOT read them equally. Look at the U-shaped recall curve from the lab:
• Chunk 1/10 (Very Top): 93.0% recall
• Chunk 6/10 (Dead Middle): 38.7% recall!
• Chunk 10/10 (Very Bottom): 93.0% recall
7/ Just like a student cramming before an exam, the model remembers the first page (primacy) and the last page (recency), while the middle blurs out.
8/ Pro rule for every prompt you write: put core rules at the very top, background filler in the middle, and your #1 most important retrieved fact + question at the very bottom.

code_walkthrough.title: FIFO Sliding Window Truncation (Why `7492` Vanishes)
code_walkthrough.why_it_matters: Walking backward from the newest turn packs the most recent messages onto the tray first. The instant `used + cost > max_words`, older messages (including Turn 1's locker code `7492`) are silently evicted — the model never even receives them.
code_walkthrough.what_if_removed: Without budget management, your API call fails with `400 context_length_exceeded` the moment a long chat crosses the model's window limit.

code_walkthrough.title: Multi-Turn Billing & The 81% KV Prefix Cache Discount
code_walkthrough.why_it_matters: Across 10 turns, uncached chat bills `19,000` input tokens because Turn 1 is re-billed 10 times (`O(T^2)` total tokens!). With KV Prefix Caching (`0.1x` cost on cached prefix), the exact same 10-turn chat drops to `3,610` effective tokens (`81.0%` cheaper).
code_walkthrough.what_if_removed: Mutating *anything* near the top of `prefix_so_far` (like a live clock or random ID) forces `cached_prefix_tokens = 0` on every turn.

code_walkthrough.title: Quadratic Causal Attention Scaling `O(N^2)`
code_walkthrough.why_it_matters: In causal self-attention, token `k` attends to all `k` tokens before it (`1 + 2 + ... + N = N(N+1)/2`). Scaling context 10x from `10k -> 100k` tokens multiplies attention pairs by **100x** (`50M -> 5.0B` pairs), driving up Time-To-First-Token (TTFT).
code_walkthrough.what_if_removed: Treating a 1M context window as 'free unlimited RAM' causes 30-second prefill stalls and severe Context Rot.

code_walkthrough.title: The Primacy/Recency U-Curve Placement Rule
code_walkthrough.why_it_matters: This analytical curve reproduces Liu et al. (2023)'s empirical discovery: recall stays high (`~93%`) at the opening and closing edges (`x = 0` and `x = 1`) and sags sharply (`~38.7%`) in the middle (`x = 0.5`).
code_walkthrough.what_if_removed: Dumping 40 retrieved RAG chunks in arbitrary order buries the single gold-nugget paragraph right in the middle dead zone.
